lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a win-win? (An idea that is good for both sides.) Groups must make choices all the time. Today: fair ways to decide together.
One person decides: quick, and fine for small things, like a team captain choosing a team name. But if others never get a say, they may feel it is unfair.
Voting: everyone gets one vote, and the choice with the most votes wins. It is fair when many people must decide. In a secret vote nobody sees how you voted, so you can choose freely.
A majority means more than half. With 30 voters, a majority is 16 or more. One idea gets 12 votes, another 10 and another 8. The first wins with the most votes, but not with a majority.
Agreeing, or consensus: the group talks until everyone can accept one choice. It takes longer, but nobody is left out. It works well in small groups, like friends planning a build.
Taking turns: when the same choice comes up again and again, like who picks the game, take turns so everyone gets a go. Picking a name from a hat is fair when every choice is equally good.
Which way is fair? Ask: How many people? How important is it? How much time is there? After a vote, respect the result, and remember that the other side's ideas still matter.

Try it in the world: with your friends, choose your next build three ways: a show of hands, a secret vote with signs, and talking until you agree. Which felt fairest? Next: keep going when things get hard.

exercises.prompt: In a vote, which choice wins?
choices: the one with the most votes
the one the loudest person likes
the one with the fewest votes
exercises.explain: The choice with the most votes wins.

exercises.prompt: In a secret vote, nobody sees how you voted.
exercises.explain: True: a secret vote lets everyone choose freely.

exercises.hint: Think of who picks the game each day.
choices: each person gets a go, one after another
exercises.explain: Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another.

exercises.hint: Split the voters into two equal groups. A majority is bigger than one of them.
exercises.explain: A majority is more than half of the votes.

exercises.prompt: There are 20 voters. How many votes make a majority?
exercises.hint: Half of 20 is 10. A majority is more than half.
exercises.explain: Half of 20 is 10, so 11 votes or more is a majority.

exercises.prompt: Match each way of deciding to when it works well.
exercises.hint: Think of how many people there are, and how much time.
exercises.explain: One person: small, quick choices. A vote: many people. Consensus: small groups with time. Turns: choices made again and again.

exercises.prompt: Three friends choose a game every day. What is a fair way?
exercises.hint: The same choice comes up again and again.
exercises.explain: Take turns: over the week, everyone gets to choose.

exercises.hint: It takes time, but nobody is left out.
choices: talking until everyone can accept one choice
exercises.explain: Consensus means talking until everyone can accept one choice.

exercises.prompt: After a fair vote, the losing side's ideas no longer matter.
exercises.hint: Respect the result. Could the other side's good ideas still help the group?
exercises.explain: False: respect the result, but the other side's ideas still matter and may help next time.

exercises.prompt: 30 children choose a class trip. Which way is fairest?
choices: a vote, so everyone has a say
exercises.explain: With many people, a vote gives everyone an equal say.

exercises.prompt: In a vote of 12, 10 and 8, the winner has a majority.
exercises.hint: Add up the votes and find half.
exercises.explain: False: 12 + 10 + 8 = 30, and half of 30 is 15. 12 is not more than 15, so it wins with the most votes but no majority.

exercises.prompt: When is picking a name from a hat a fair way to decide?
exercises.hint: Would you pick from a hat when one choice is clearly better?
choices: when every choice is equally good
when one choice is clearly best
exercises.explain: A draw is fair when all the choices are equally good; for choices that matter, talking or voting is better.

exercises.prompt: Two friends want different names for their shared pet. What could they do?
choices: find a name both like, or mix their ideas
exercises.explain: They can talk until they agree, perhaps mixing their ideas: a win-win.

exercises.prompt: In a vote, 9 children chose the pond, 6 the maze and 5 the tower. How many more votes would the pond have needed for a majority?
exercises.hint: Add up all the votes, find a majority, then compare it with the pond's 9.
exercises.explain: 9 + 6 + 5 = 20 voters, so a majority is 11. 11 − 9 = 2 more votes.

exercises.prompt: Sort the choices by the fairest way to make them.
items: who picks the game each day
a school chooses a council member
who goes first on the swing
exercises.hint: Many people: vote. A choice made again and again: turns. A small group with time: talk until all agree.
exercises.explain: A vote: the class trip and the council member (many people). Take turns: the daily game and the swing. Consensus: the shared build and the pet's name (a small group with time).

exercises.prompt: A vote: the pond 9, the maze 6, the tower 5. Sort the statements: true or false?
items: The pond won the most votes.
exercises.hint: Add the votes first, then find half.
exercises.explain: 9 + 6 + 5 = 20 voters, so a majority is 11 or more. The pond won the most votes (9), but 9 is not a majority.
